extracted.intended_audience: general readers; writers and publishing professionals interested in author biography and memoir ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of standards, ethical expectations, and procedural consequences around marketing and publishing memoirs — focused on factual accuracy, publisher responsibilities, and remedies when a memoir is found to contain fabrications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoir factual accuracy / authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Books marketed as memoirs should accurately represent factual events; Frey's A Million Little Pieces and My Friend Leonard were initially marketed as memoirs but were later found to contain large exaggerations or fabrications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents that the Smoking Gun alleged large invented portions of Frey's memoirs (e.g., overstated incarceration), and that Frey later admitted some allegations were true while claiming memoirs alter minor details for literary effect. The surrounding narrative shows that major fabrications undermine a work's classification as memoir and provoke media and legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher responsibility to verify and classify genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should appropriately verify factual claims and accurately classify works as memoir or fiction; Frey's publishers initially stood by the memoir classification but later altered their stance and added disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nan Talese (publisher) admitted she had done nothing to check the book's veracity despite assurances. The publishers later included a publisher's note and an author's note as disclaimers. Misclassification led to dropped deals, reputational harm, and legal settlement activity documented on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media/endorser due diligence (e.g., Oprah's vetting role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public endorsers and media platforms should perform or rely on due diligence when promoting memoirs or other purportedly factual works; Oprah relied on the publisher to assess authenticity and later faced backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recounts Oprah's selection of A Million Little Pieces for her book club, her on-air interviews with Frey when controversy arose, and subsequent apology — demonstrating that endorsement without adequate verification can produce reputational cost and public controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial/legal remedies and reader restitution procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When readers claim they were deceived by a work marketed as a memoir, publishers may offer refunds under settlement terms that define eligibility and required proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Random House/settlement required customers to submit proof of purchase (e.g., page 163 from hardcover or front cover from paperback) and complete a sworn statement indicating they purchased the book under the assumption it was a memoir. The settlement set aside funds but relatively few claimants ultimately received refunds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of publisher's/author's note or disclaimers when veracity is contested
rubrics_metrics.description: If significant factual issues are revealed, publishers may add a publisher's note and/or an author's note to subsequent editions to disclose the somewhat fictitious nature of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After examining evidence, publishers added disclaimers to later publications of Frey's book. The page presents this as a response to discovered fabrications and as a mitigation measure to inform future readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of author contracts and credit/compensation terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing contracts should avoid overly restrictive terms that permit removal, deny credit, or provide negligible compensation; Frey's Full Fathom Five contract was criticized for allowing removal of an author at any time, not requiring credit, and offering a standard advance of $250.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page details controversy when an MFA student was released from an 'extremely limiting contract' for FFF, and public criticism labeled the contract exploitative. This functions as an anti-pattern: contracts that grant a company unilateral rights and minimal pay invite ethical and reputational criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical labor practices in commercial fiction production
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial publishing ventures should avoid exploiting inexperienced writers (e.g., MFA students) as cheap labor to churn out work; allegations arose that Frey used MFA students in such a way for young-adult novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York magazine and other outlets reported that Frey 'abused and used MFA students as cheap labor' in his effort to build highly commercial novels. The page frames this as a problematic practice that drew controversy and harmed reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of misrepresenting genre (memoir vs fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresenting a fictionalized narrative as a memoir can lead to loss of support, cancelled deals, legal action, refunds, and sustained media controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces consequences experienced by Frey: dropped literary manager, cancelled deals (Riverhead Books dropping a two-book deal), legal settlement with refund offers, public apologies, and long-term reputational effects (parodies, critical coverage). This illustrates why accurate genre representation matters.
